claims.text: The corrosion resistance of these steels is governed by a stable chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer is primarily Cr2O3.
The chromium-rich passive layer forms on the steel surface during processing.
The chromium-rich passive layer is self-healing.
The passive layer significantly reduces corrosion by acting as a barrier to aggressive ions and molecules.
A controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment in air promotes formation of a uniform, adherent chromium-rich oxide film.
A chromium content of at least 12% is adequate for the proposed passivation behavior in high-alloy steels.
Standard annealing homogenizes the microstructure of the conventionally processed steel.
The oxidation pretreatment produces a continuous and adherent Cr2O3 passive film.
The Cr2O3 film limits diffusion of chlorides and protons to the underlying steel matrix.
Limiting transport of corrosive species minimizes anodic metal dissolution.
Reducing anodic metal dissolution retards the overall corrosion process.
Pre-oxidized specimens with a robust Cr2O3 film will have lower corrosion rates than untreated specimens or lower-chromium steels.
The lower corrosion rate will appear as reduced weight loss, lower pit density, or diminished electrochemical current.
Untreated steels or steels with lower effective chromium content lack a well-formed passivating oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism applies when chromium is at least approximately 12% and service conditions remain below passive-film breakdown thresholds.
Temperatures well below 150°C and industrially relevant chloride concentrations are within the regime where the passive film remains protective.
Molybdenum or nickel may synergistically enhance chromium-based passivation.
Long-term thermal, mechanical, and radiation cycling may affect passive-film stability.
Comparable corrosion behavior in oxide-removed and pre-oxidized samples would falsify the claim that the Cr2O3 film is the governing protective mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mediator is claimed to self-repair after damage, but the falsification experiment treats abrasion or oxide removal as creating a persistently film-free control. Similar corrosion behavior could result from passive-film regrowth on the abraded samples and therefore would not, by itself, falsify the film mechanism.
